**Magnum Photos** is an international photographic [cooperative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative "Cooperative") owned by its photographer-members, with offices in Paris, New York City and London. It was founded in 1947 in Paris by photographers [Robert Capa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Capa "Robert Capa"), [David "Chim" Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Seymour_(photographer) "David Seymour (photographer)"), [Maria Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Eisner "Maria Eisner"), [Henri Cartier-Bresson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Cartier-Bresson "Henri Cartier-Bresson"), [George Rodger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Rodger "George Rodger"), [William Vandivert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Vandivert "William Vandivert"), and Rita Vandivert. Its photographers retain all copyrights to their own work.

In 2010, [MSD Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DFO_Management "DFO Management") acquired a collection of nearly 200,000 original press prints of images taken by Magnum photographers, which in 2013 it donated to the [Harry Ransom Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Ransom_Center "Harry Ransom Center").

Magnum was founded in Paris in 1947 by [Robert Capa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Capa "Robert Capa"), [David "Chim" Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Seymour_(photographer) "David Seymour (photographer)"), [Henri Cartier-Bresson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Cartier-Bresson "Henri Cartier-Bresson"), [George Rodger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Rodger "George Rodger") and [William Vandivert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Vandivert "William Vandivert") (all photographers), Rita Vandivert and [Maria Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Eisner "Maria Eisner"), based on an idea of Capa's. (Seymour, Cartier-Bresson and Rodger were all absent from the meeting at which it was founded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-1) In response to a letter telling him that he was a member, Rodger wrote that Magnum seemed a good idea but, "It all sounded too halcyon to be true," when Capa had told him of it and, "I rather dismissed the whole thing from my mind".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-2))

Rita Vandivert was the cooperative's first president and head of the New York office, while Maria Eisner headed the Paris office.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-Miller,_Magnum,_p.51-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-4) The plan was for Rodger to cover Africa and the Middle East; Cartier-Bresson to cover south and east Asia; Seymour and William Vandivert to cover Europe and the United States, respectively; and Capa to be free to follow his curiosity and events.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-Miller,_Magnum,_p.51-3)

Magnum is one of the first photographic [cooperatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperatives "Cooperatives"), owned and administered entirely by members. The staff serve a support role for the photographers, who retain all copyrights to the photographs they take.

The Magnum cooperative has included [photojournalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photojournalism "Photojournalism") from across the world who have covered many historical events of the 20th century. The cooperative's archive includes photographs depicting family life, [drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoactive_drug "Psychoactive drug"), religion, war, poverty, [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine"), crime, government and [celebrities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity "Celebrity").

Although it has been asserted that the name "Magnum" was chosen because the founding members always drank a bottle of champagne during the first meetings,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-5)[Russell Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Miller "Russell Miller") writes:

> It was . . . presumably agreed by those present [at the first meeting] that Magnum was a fine new name for such a bold new venture, indicative as it was of greatness in its literal Latin translation, toughness in its gun connotation and celebration in its champagne mode.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-6)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Boy_destroying_piano.jpg/250px-Boy_destroying_piano.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boy_destroying_piano.jpg)

Boy destroying piano at Pant-y-Waen, South Wales, by [Philip Jones Griffiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Jones_Griffiths "Philip Jones Griffiths"), 1961

Magnum is owned by its photographers, who act as shareholders. Each full member of Magnum has a vote in proposals made at a meeting held once a year, called the Annual General Meeting (AGM).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-magnumphotos_AGM-8) Photographers with the status of contributor or correspondent are represented by Magnum but have no voting rights. Full members can choose to become contributors after 23 years of membership; this status gives them increased liberty to work outside Magnum, at the cost of their voting rights.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-9)

## Elections of new members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnum_Photos&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Elections of new members")]

[Video 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/Magnum%2C_Our_Own_Agency.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=rest&utm_content=original)

Interview with [Abbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbas_(photographer) "Abbas (photographer)") about Magnum

In the early years of Magnum, membership had generally come about by the personal invitation of [Robert Capa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Capa "Robert Capa"). However, in 1955 a three-stage membership system was set up that continues to this day[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-10) and is described below. Until 1953 there were also a large number of [stringers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stringer_(journalism) "Stringer (journalism)") who used Magnum but were not members.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-11)

Magnum's photographers meet once a year, during the last weekend in June, in New York City, Paris or London, to discuss the cooperative's business. One day of the meeting is reserved to review potential new members' portfolios and vote on admitting individuals. An approved applicant is invited to become a 'Nominee Member' of Magnum, a category of membership that provides a chance for members and the individual to get to know each other, but that includes no binding commitments on either side.

After two years of Nominee membership, a photographer may present another portfolio if wanting to apply for 'Associate Membership'. If successful, the photographer is bound by the rules of the agency, and enjoys its facilities and worldwide representation. The difference between an Associate Member and a full Member is that an Associate is not a Director of the Company and does not have voting rights in the corporate decision-making. After two more years, an Associate wanting to be considered for full membership presents another portfolio of work for consideration by the members. Once elected as a full member, the individual is a member of Magnum for life or for as long as the photographer chooses.

## Accusations of child abuse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnum_Photos&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Accusations of child abuse")]

Magnum Photos' digital archive constitutes more than 1 million images, which Magnum licenses through its website.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-theguardian-beaumont-12) In August 2020, the Magnum website was taken offline after issues were raised by the _Fstoppers_ photography website and amplified on social media by others including [Jörg Colberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6rg_Colberg "Jörg Colberg"). Given the tags on the photos, there was concern that Magnum was making available photographs of children featuring nudity; that documented encounters that constituted a record of acts of child sexual abuse; and that were problematic[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] in terms of the way they had been labelled for searching.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-theguardian-beaumont-12) "Much of the criticism [...] has focused on a series of photographs by the US photographer [David Alan Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Alan_Harvey "David Alan Harvey") from his time documenting sex workers in Bangkok in 1989."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-14) In a statement Magnum said it will re-examine the content of its archive, and has since made its website available again but without Harvey's Bangkok series.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-theguardian-beaumont-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-15) Harvey was later suspended for a year following a formal investigation into sexual misconduct allegations against him.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-CJR-16)

## Photographic collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Magnum_Photos&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Photographic collection")]

In February 2010, Magnum announced that [Michael Dell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Dell "Michael Dell")'s venture capital firm MSD Capital had acquired a collection of nearly 200,000 original press prints of images taken by Magnum photographers. It had formed a partnership with the [Harry Ransom Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Ransom_Center "Harry Ransom Center") at [The University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_University_of_Texas_at_Austin "The University of Texas at Austin") to preserve, catalog, and make photographs available to the general public.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-19) In September 2013 it was announced MSD Capital donated the collection to the Ransom Center.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-20) A preliminary inventory is available for researchers who wish to use the collection.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_Photos#cite_note-21)
